name: The Premack Principle
statement: A more-probable, preferred behavior can reinforce a less-probable one, so access to the favored activity is made contingent on the lesser.
meaning: The Premack principle says reinforcement is relative, not absolute: any higher-probability behavior can serve as a reinforcer for a lower-probability behavior. It shifts the focus from special "reward" stimuli to the relative value of activities themselves. Colloquially it is "grandma's rule": first do the less-preferred task, then the preferred one.
mechanism: When engaging in a high-probability behavior is made contingent on first performing a low-probability behavior, the rate of the low-probability behavior increases. Preference — measured as the baseline probability of engaging in each behavior — determines which activity reinforces which, and the relationship reverses if preferences reverse.

examples.text: Premack found that for children who preferred candy, requiring pinball-play to earn candy reinforced pinball; for children who preferred pinball, the contingency reversed as the principle predicts.
"Finish your vegetables, then you can have dessert" uses the more-probable behavior (eating dessert) to reinforce the less-probable one (eating vegetables).
A teacher lets students have free playtime only after completing worksheets, using the preferred activity to increase the less-preferred one.

whyItMatters: The principle is a workhorse of applied behavior analysis, special education, and parenting, giving a practical, individualized way to pick reinforcers. It reframed reinforcement as a relationship between behaviors rather than a property of stimuli.
limits: Timberlake and Allison's 1974 response-deprivation theory showed reinforcement depends on restricting a behavior below its baseline level, not merely on relative probability, and can explain cases the Premack principle cannot. Probabilities can also shift with satiation and context, complicating prediction.
misreadings: It does not claim a behavior is "rewarding" in the abstract; whether an activity reinforces depends on the individual's current relative preferences.
origin: Set out by David Premack in "Toward empirical behavior laws: I. Positive reinforcement", Psychological Review 66(4), 1959, and developed through the 1960s in studies of monkeys, rats and children. Premack's move was to stop treating reinforcers as a special class of thing — food, water, praise — and treat reinforcement as a relation between behaviours: whichever activity an animal freely does more of can reinforce whichever it does less of.

sources.text: Premack, D. (1959). "Toward empirical behavior laws: I. Positive reinforcement." Psychological Review 66(4), p. 219.
Wikipedia's "Premack's principle" article — supports the attribution to David Premack, the definition that more-probable behaviors reinforce less-probable ones, and the response-deprivation critique.
Simply Psychology's "The Premack Principle" — supports the definition that a more desirable activity can reinforce a less desirable one and its use in applied settings.
